Question 01: Hidden Markov Model​

To solve these questions, we assume an initial uniform distribution for the weather on Day 1 (P(S1)=P(R1)=P(C1)=1/3P(S_1) = P(R_1) = P(C_1) = 1/3P(S1​)=P(R1​)=P(C1​)=1/3) since no starting probabilities were provided in the prompt.

(a) Determine the most likely sequence of weather states corresponding to the observed activities.

To find the most likely sequence for the observations Jogging (O1O_1O1​), Shopping (O2O_2O2​), Stays Indoors (O3O_3O3​), we use the Viterbi Algorithm.

Day 1: Observation = Jogging

We calculate v1(k)=P(O1∣k)⋅P(k)v_1(k) = P(O_1|k) \cdot P(k)v1​(k)=P(O1​∣k)⋅P(k):

  • Sunny: 0.7×0.333=0.23310.7 \times 0.333 = 0.23310.7×0.333=0.2331
  • Rainy: 0.1×0.333=0.03330.1 \times 0.333 = 0.03330.1×0.333=0.0333
  • Cloudy: 0.2×0.333=0.06660.2 \times 0.333 = 0.06660.2×0.333=0.0666

Day 2: Observation = Shopping

We calculate v2(k)=P(O2∣k)⋅max⁡j(v1(j)⋅P(k∣j))v_2(k) = P(O_2|k) \cdot \max_{j}(v_1(j) \cdot P(k|j))v2​(k)=P(O2​∣k)⋅maxj​(v1​(j)⋅P(k∣j)):

  • Sunny: 0.2×max⁡(0.2331⋅0.6,0.0333⋅0.2,0.0666⋅0.3)=0.2×0.13986=0.027970.2 \times \max(0.2331 \cdot 0.6, 0.0333 \cdot 0.2, 0.0666 \cdot 0.3) = 0.2 \times 0.13986 = \mathbf{0.02797}0.2×max(0.2331⋅0.6,0.0333⋅0.2,0.0666⋅0.3)=0.2×0.13986=0.02797 (from Sunny)
  • Rainy: 0.4×max⁡(0.2331⋅0.1,0.0333⋅0.7,0.0666⋅0.3)=0.4×0.02331=0.009320.4 \times \max(0.2331 \cdot 0.1, 0.0333 \cdot 0.7, 0.0666 \cdot 0.3) = 0.4 \times 0.02331 = \mathbf{0.00932}0.4×max(0.2331⋅0.1,0.0333⋅0.7,0.0666⋅0.3)=0.4×0.02331=0.00932 (from Sunny or Rainy)

We calculate v3(k)=P(O3∣k)⋅max⁡j(v2(j)⋅P(k∣j))v_3(k) = P(O_3|k) \cdot \max_{j}(v_2(j) \cdot P(k|j))v3​(k)=P(O3​∣k)⋅maxj​(v2​(j)⋅P(k∣j)):

(c) After the observation sequence, what is the posterior probability of the weather on the third day being Cloudy?

The posterior probability for a state on a specific day is the forward probability for that state divided by the total probability of the sequence.

P(S3=Cloudy∣O1:3)=α3(Cloudy)P(O1:3)P(S_3 = \text{Cloudy} | O_{1:3}) = \frac{\alpha_3(\text{Cloudy})}{P(O_{1:3})}P(S3​=Cloudy∣O1:3​)=P(O1:3​)α3​(Cloudy)​

  • α3(Cloudy)=0.0123\alpha_3(\text{Cloudy}) = 0.0123α3​(Cloudy)=0.0123
  • P(O1:3)=0.03118P(O_{1:3}) = 0.03118P(O1:3​)=0.03118

Posterior Probability: 0.01230.03118≈0.3945\frac{0.0123}{0.03118} \approx \mathbf{0.3945}0.031180.0123​≈0.3945 (or 39.45%).

Question 02: Entropy​

(a) Calculate the entropy of the entire dataset.

Entropy measures the "impurity" or randomness in the target variable (Buy). The formula for Entropy is:

E(S)=∑i=1c−pilog⁡2(pi)E(S) = \sum_{i=1}^{c} -p_i \log_2(p_i)E(S)=∑i=1c​−pi​log2​(pi​)

In our dataset of 6 samples:

  • Total Samples (nnn): 6
  • Buy = Yes: 3 (IDs 2, 3, 4)
  • Buy = No: 3 (IDs 1, 5, 6)

Since the split is exactly 50/5050/5050/50, the entropy will be 1:

E(S)=−(36)log⁡2(36)−(36)log⁡2(36)E(S) = -\left(\frac{3}{6}\right) \log_2 \left(\frac{3}{6}\right) - \left(\frac{3}{6}\right) \log_2 \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)E(S)=−(63​)log2​(63​)−(63​)log2​(63​)

E(S)=−0.5(−1)−0.5(−1)=1.0E(S) = -0.5(-1) - 0.5(-1) = \mathbf{1.0}E(S)=−0.5(−1)−0.5(−1)=1.0

Root Node: Income has the highest Information Gain (0.5410.5410.541).

The Decision Tree Structure

  1. Income = Medium: Always Yes (Node is pure).
  2. Income = Low: Always No (Node is pure).
  3. Income = High: This node contains IDs 1, 2, and 3. We must split again.

  • IDs at node: 1 (No), 2 (Yes), 3 (No). (Wait, looking at data: ID 1: Young/High/No=No, ID 2: Young/High/Yes=Yes, ID 3: Young/High/No=Yes).

  • In the Income=High branch, if we split by Previous Purchases:

  • Prev = Yes: ID 2 →\rightarrow→ Buy: Yes

  • Prev = No: ID 1 and 3 →\rightarrow→ Buy: No, Yes (Mixed results).

  • Since no further splits can perfectly separate ID 1 and 3 (they have identical features but different outcomes), we stop here and take the majority class for the mixed leaf.

Class Test 02​

Question 01: Regression Model​

(a) Explain how each model behaves in terms of bias and variance.

Model A: Simple Linear Regression (only two features)

Characteristics

  • Uses only 2 features.
  • Assumes a linear relationship.
  • Very simple model.

Bias and Variance

  • Bias: High (cannot capture complex relationships).
  • Variance: Low (predictions are stable across different training sets).

Result

  • May underfit the data.

Answer:

  • High Bias
  • Low Variance
  • Likely to underfit because it ignores many useful features.

Model B: Polynomial Regression (Degree 3)

Characteristics

  • Uses all features.
  • Includes polynomial (cubic) terms.
  • Can model nonlinear relationships.

Bias and Variance

  • Bias: Lower than Model A.
  • Variance: Higher because the model is more flexible.

Result

  • Fits training data well.
  • Can overfit if the dataset is small or noisy.

Answer

  • Moderate/Low Bias
  • High Variance
  • May overfit the training data.

Model C: Random Forest Regressor

Characteristics

  • Uses many decision trees.
  • Predictions are averaged across trees.
  • Hyperparameters are optimized.

Bias and Variance

  • Bias: Low.
  • Variance: Lower than a single decision tree because averaging reduces variance.

Result

  • Usually provides the best balance between bias and variance.

Answer

  • Low Bias
  • Moderate/Low Variance
  • Good generalization performance.
ModelBiasVarianceLikely Problem
Model A (Linear Regression)HighLowUnderfitting
Model B (Polynomial Degree 3)LowHighOverfitting
Model C (Random Forest)LowModerate/LowBest balance
(b) How would overfitting affect Model B?

Overfitting occurs when the model learns:

  • actual patterns and
  • random noise in the training data.

As a result, it performs well on training data but poorly on unseen data.

Effect on Model B

Since Model B is flexible, it may:

  • Fit the training data extremely well.
  • Capture noise instead of the true relationship.
  • Give poor predictions on new patients.

Evidence of Overfitting

Look for:

  1. Very low training error
  2. High validation/test error
  3. Large gap between training and testing performance.

Example:

DatasetRMSE
Training2
Testing12

The large difference indicates overfitting.

Model B may overfit by memorizing noise in the training data, leading to excellent training accuracy but poor test performance. Evidence includes a low training error and a much higher validation/test error, indicating poor generalization.

(c) Which evaluation strategy should be used?

Use k-Fold Cross-Validation

A common choice is k-Fold Cross-Validation (e.g., 5-fold or 10-fold).

Procedure:

  1. Split the dataset into k equal parts.
  2. Train on k−1 folds.
  3. Test on the remaining fold.
  4. Repeat until every fold has been used as the test set.
  5. Compute the average performance.

Why use Cross-Validation?

It:

  • Uses all data for both training and testing.
  • Provides a reliable estimate of model performance.
  • Detects overfitting and underfitting.
  • Helps compare all three models fairly.

Evaluation Metrics

Use regression metrics such as:

  • Mean Squared Error (MSE)
  • Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
  • Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
  • (R^2) Score

Choose the model with:

  • Lowest RMSE/MAE
  • Highest (R^2)
  • Small difference between training and validation performance

Use k-Fold Cross-Validation (5-fold or 10-fold) with regression metrics such as RMSE, MAE, MSE, and (R^2). This strategy provides a reliable estimate of performance, helps detect overfitting, and ensures a good bias–variance trade-off by comparing the average validation performance of all three models.

Question 01: Decision Tree Calculations​

(a) Calculate the information gain (IG) of the split made at the root node.

Information Gain is calculated as:

IG=Entropy(Parent)−[Weighted Average Entropy(Children)]IG = Entropy(\text{Parent}) - [Weighted\ Average\ Entropy(\text{Children})]IG=Entropy(Parent)−[Weighted Average Entropy(Children)]

  1. Root Entropy: −(16/32)log⁡2(16/32)−(16/32)log⁡2(16/32)=1.0-(16/32)\log_2(16/32) - (16/32)\log_2(16/32) = \mathbf{1.0}−(16/32)log2​(16/32)−(16/32)log2​(16/32)=1.0
  2. Left Child Entropy (12, 4): −(12/16)log⁡2(12/16)−(4/16)log⁡2(4/16)≈0.811-(12/16)\log_2(12/16) - (4/16)\log_2(4/16) \approx \mathbf{0.811}−(12/16)log2​(12/16)−(4/16)log2​(4/16)≈0.811
  3. Right Child Entropy (4, 12): −(4/16)log⁡2(4/16)−(12/16)log⁡2(12/16)≈0.811-(4/16)\log_2(4/16) - (12/16)\log_2(12/16) \approx \mathbf{0.811}−(4/16)log2​(4/16)−(12/16)log2​(12/16)≈0.811
  4. Weighted Child Entropy: (16/32×0.811)+(16/32×0.811)=0.811(16/32 \times 0.811) + (16/32 \times 0.811) = 0.811(16/32×0.811)+(16/32×0.811)=0.811
  5. IG: 1.0−0.811=0.1891.0 - 0.811 = \mathbf{0.189}1.0−0.811=0.189
(b) Determine the values of aaa and bbb for smallest IG, and xxx and yyy for largest IG.

Information Gain (IG) is a measure used in decision tree algorithms (such as ID3 and C4.5) to determine the best attribute for splitting a node. It measures the reduction in uncertainty (entropy) after a split.

The formula for Information Gain is:

IG=Entropy(Parent)−Weighted Entropy(Children)\boxed{\text{IG}=\text{Entropy(Parent)}-\text{Weighted Entropy(Children)}}IG=Entropy(Parent)−Weighted Entropy(Children)​

Where:

  • Entropy(Parent) is the impurity before splitting.
  • Weighted Entropy(Children) is the combined impurity of the child nodes after splitting.

A good split reduces entropy, resulting in a high Information Gain.

Smallest Information Gain

The smallest possible Information Gain is 0.

This occurs when the split does not reduce entropy. In other words:

  • The child nodes have the same class distribution as the parent node.
  • The weighted entropy of the child nodes is equal to the entropy of the parent node.

Mathematically,

Entropy(Parent)=Weighted Entropy(Children)\text{Entropy(Parent)}=\text{Weighted Entropy(Children)}Entropy(Parent)=Weighted Entropy(Children)

Therefore,

IG=0\boxed{\text{IG}=0}IG=0​

Applying this to the given tree

The left parent node contains

(12,4)(12,4)(12,4)

The class ratio is

12:4=3:112:4=3:112:4=3:1

To keep the entropy unchanged, the child nodes must also have the same ratio (3:1).

Choose

a=9,b=3\boxed{a=9,\qquad b=3}a=9,b=3​

The remaining child becomes

(12−9,4−3)=(3,1)(12-9,4-3)=(3,1)(12−9,4−3)=(3,1)

Both child nodes have the ratio

9:3=3:19:3=3:19:3=3:1

and

3:1=3:13:1=3:13:1=3:1

Since both children have the same class distribution as the parent, the entropy does not change.

Hence,

a=9,b=3\boxed{a=9,b=3}a=9,b=3​

gives the smallest Information Gain (IG = 0).

Largest Information Gain

The largest Information Gain occurs when the split completely removes uncertainty.

This happens when:

  • Each child node is pure, meaning it contains instances of only one class.
  • The entropy of each child node is 0.

Thus,

Weighted Entropy(Children)=0\text{Weighted Entropy(Children)}=0Weighted Entropy(Children)=0

Therefore,

IG=Entropy(Parent)\boxed{\text{IG}=\text{Entropy(Parent)}}IG=Entropy(Parent)​

which is the maximum possible Information Gain.

Applying this to the given tree

The right parent node contains

(4,12)(4,12)(4,12)

To obtain pure child nodes:

  • Put all positive examples into one child.
  • Put all negative examples into the other child.

Choose

x=4,y=0\boxed{x=4,\qquad y=0}x=4,y=0​

The remaining child becomes

(4−4,12−0)=(0,12)(4-4,12-0)=(0,12)(4−4,12−0)=(0,12)

The two child nodes are:

  • First child: (4,0) → only positive examples (pure)
  • Second child: (0,12) → only negative examples (pure)

Since both child nodes have zero entropy, the weighted entropy after splitting is zero, producing the maximum Information Gain.

Thus,

x=4,y=0\boxed{x=4,y=0}x=4,y=0​
(c) Discuss three potential ways for reducing overfitting in a decision tree.

Overfitting in a decision tree occurs when the tree learns the training data too closely, including noise and outliers, which reduces its performance on new, unseen data. Three common ways to reduce overfitting are:

  1. Pruning the Tree
    • Pruning removes branches that contribute little to improving prediction accuracy.
    • Pre-pruning (Early Stopping): Stops the tree from growing beyond a certain point by setting limits such as maximum depth or minimum samples required to split a node.
    • Post-pruning: Allows the tree to grow fully and then removes unnecessary branches based on validation performance.
    • Benefit: Produces a simpler model that generalizes better.
  2. Limiting Tree Depth
    • Restrict the maximum depth of the decision tree.
    • A very deep tree tends to memorize the training data, while a shallower tree captures only the most important patterns.
    • Benefit: Reduces model complexity and lowers the risk of fitting noise in the data.
  3. Setting Minimum Samples for Splitting or Leaf Nodes
    • Specify a minimum number of samples required to split an internal node or to remain in a leaf node.
    • This prevents the tree from creating branches based on very few observations, which are often caused by random variations.
    • Benefit: Leads to more reliable splits and improves the model's ability to generalize.

These techniques pruning, limiting tree depth, and requiring a minimum number of samples for splits or leaf nodes help create simpler decision trees that are less likely to overfit and more likely to perform well on unseen data.

Question 02: ANN + SVM​

(a) Design a Neural Network

Observe the data

From the figure:

  • Crosses (✚) are clustered in the center.
  • Diamonds (◇) surround the crosses from all sides.

This means:

  • The classes cannot be separated by a single straight line.
  • A closed boundary (box or circle) is needed around the center.

Hence, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with one hidden layer is required.

Choose the Network

A suitable architecture is

Architecture:

  • Input layer: 2 neurons (x1, x2)
  • Hidden layer: 4 neurons
  • Output layer: 1 neuron

Hence,

2−4−1 MLP\boxed{2-4-1 \text{ MLP}}2−4−1 MLP​

Why 4 Hidden Neurons?

Each hidden neuron can learn one linear boundary.

Four neurons can create

  • Left boundary
  • Right boundary
  • Upper boundary
  • Lower boundary

Together they form a rectangle enclosing the crosses.

The output neuron performs an AND operation:

  • If all four conditions are satisfied → classify as Cross
  • Otherwise → classify as Diamond

Decision Boundary

The decision boundary would look like

        ◇   ◇   ◇

      ◇ ┌────────┐ ◇
         │ ✚ ✚ ✚│
    ◇   │ ✚ ✚ ✚ │   ◇
         │ ✚ ✚ ✚│
      ◇ └────────┘ ◇

   ◇      ◇    ◇
  • Everything inside the rectangle → Cross
  • Everything outside → Diamond
(b) Hard Margin SVM

What is Hard Margin SVM?

Hard-margin SVM tries to find one straight hyperplane

wTx+b=0w^Tx+b=0wTx+b=0

that perfectly separates the two classes.

Why does it fail here?

The data is arranged as

     Diamonds

 Diamonds  Crosses Diamonds

     Diamonds

The crosses are completely surrounded by diamonds. No single straight line can separate them. Hence, Data is not linearly separable.

Therefore, Hard-margin SVM fails.

Kernel Trick

Instead of separating data in the original 2D space, the kernel maps the data into a higher-dimensional feature space.

Suppose we transform

(x1,x2)(x_1,x_2)(x1​,x2​)

into

(x1,x2,x12+x22)(x_1,x_2,x_1^2+x_2^2)(x1​,x2​,x12​+x22​)

In this higher-dimensional space,

  • the two classes become linearly separable.
  • then SVM finds a linear hyperplane there.
  • when mapped back to the original space,
  • the boundary becomes non-linear (circle/ellipse).

Suitable Kernel

The most suitable kernels are:

  • Polynomial Kernel
  • Radial Basis Function (RBF/Gaussian) Kernel

The RBF kernel is the most common choice because it naturally creates a circular decision boundary around the central cluster.

Decision Boundary

SVM with RBF

      ○ ✚ ○

The circular boundary separates the center (crosses) from the surrounding diamonds.

For K=0K=0K=0:

(b) Construct a test sample for which Naïve Bayes Classifier fails to classify without Laplacian Smoothing. Explain how Laplacian Smoothing assists.

Test Sample: X=1,Y=1,Z=0X=1, Y=1, Z=0X=1,Y=1,Z=0.

The Problem:

Looking at the data for K=1K=1K=1, there are zero instances where Y=1Y=1Y=1 AND K=1K=1K=1 simultaneously (Wait, looking closely at the table: row 2 and 4 show Y=1Y=1Y=1 when K=1K=1K=1). Let's look for a true zero: In the data, for K=1K=1K=1, ZZZ is always 111. Therefore, P(Z=0∣K=1)=0P(Z=0|K=1) = 0P(Z=0∣K=1)=0.

If we test a sample where Z=0Z=0Z=0, the entire product for K=1K=1K=1 becomes zero, regardless of how strong the other evidence is. This "zero-frequency" problem makes the model ignore other features.

How Laplacian Smoothing assists: It adds a small smoothing parameter (usually α=1\alpha = 1α=1) to the numerator and adjusts the denominator by the number of possible values for that feature.

P(xi∣K)=count(xi,K)+1count(K)+number of possible values of xiP(x_i|K) = \frac{count(x_i, K) + 1}{count(K) + \text{number of possible values of } x_i}P(xi​∣K)=count(K)+number of possible values of xi​count(xi​,K)+1​

This ensures no probability is ever exactly zero, allowing the classifier to still weigh the evidence from XXX and YYY.

(b) For a binary classification task, what will be the training error for a 1-Nearest Neighbor? Briefly explain.

For a 1-Nearest Neighbor (1-NN) classifier, the training error is 0% (zero), assuming there are no duplicate training samples with different class labels.

  • In the 1-NN algorithm, to classify a training example, the algorithm finds the closest training point.
  • Since each training sample is its own nearest neighbor (distance = 0), it is assigned its own class label.
  • Therefore, every training example is classified correctly, resulting in no training errors.

If the dataset contains duplicate feature vectors with conflicting class labels, then some training points cannot all be classified correctly, and the training error may be greater than 0.

(c) Discuss why kkk-Nearest Neighbors is called a "lazy learner.

kkk-NN is a lazy learner because it does not perform any "learning" or generalize a model during the training phase.

  1. No Training Phase: It simply stores the training data in memory.
  2. Computation at Test Time: All the heavy lifting (calculating distances and searching for neighbors) happens only when a prediction is requested for a new test point.
  3. Contrast: This is the opposite of "eager learners" (like Neural Networks or Decision Trees) which build a model first and then use that model to make rapid predictions.

Question 07: Random Forest​

(a) General principle of an Ensemble Method. What are Bagging and Boosting?

General Principle of Ensemble Method

An ensemble method is a machine learning technique that combines the predictions of multiple models (called weak learners or base learners) to produce a better overall prediction than any single model.

Principle:

  • Train several models instead of one.
  • Combine their outputs.
  • The combined model has higher accuracy, better stability, and lower error.

Advantages:

  • Improves prediction accuracy.
  • Reduces overfitting.
  • Increases robustness.
  • Handles complex data better.

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating)

Bagging is an ensemble technique in which multiple models are trained independently on different bootstrap (randomly sampled with replacement) datasets, and their predictions are combined.

Working:

  1. Draw several bootstrap samples from the training data.
  2. Train one model (usually a decision tree) on each sample.
  3. Combine predictions:
    • Classification: Majority voting.
    • Regression: Average of predictions.

Characteristics:

  • Models are trained in parallel.
  • Reduces variance.
  • Prevents overfitting.
  • Example: Random Forest.

Boosting

Boosting is an ensemble technique where models are trained sequentially, and each new model focuses more on the mistakes made by the previous model.

Working:

  1. Train the first weak learner.
  2. Increase the weight of incorrectly classified samples.
  3. Train the next learner on the updated data.
  4. Repeat the process.
  5. Combine all learners using weighted voting.

Characteristics:

  • Models are trained one after another.
  • Reduces bias.
  • Produces a strong learner from many weak learners.
  • Examples:
    • AdaBoost
    • Gradient Boosting
    • XGBoost

Difference between Bagging and Boosting

BaggingBoosting
Models trained independentlyModels trained sequentially
Uses bootstrap samplingUses weighted data
Reduces varianceReduces bias
Parallel trainingSequential training
Example: Random ForestExample: AdaBoost, XGBoost
(b) Effects of Changing the Number of Trees in a Random Forest

The number of trees is an important hyperparameter in Random Forest.

Case 1: Too Few Trees

  • High variance.
  • Predictions are unstable.
  • Lower accuracy.
  • Model depends heavily on a few trees.

Case 2: Increasing the Number of Trees

As the number of trees increases:

  • Accuracy generally improves.
  • Variance decreases.
  • Predictions become more stable.
  • Generalization improves.
  • Overfitting usually does not increase significantly.

Very Large Number of Trees

Advantages:

  • Stable predictions.
  • Very low variance.
  • Better performance.

Disadvantages:

  • Longer training time.
  • Higher memory usage.
  • Slower prediction speed.
  • After a certain point, accuracy improves very little (diminishing returns).
Number of TreesEffect
Too fewHigh variance, poor accuracy
ModerateBetter accuracy and stability
Very manyStable predictions but higher computation; little extra accuracy
(c) Mr. Gibson's Random Forest
  • Number of trees = 10,000
  • Training error = 0.00
  • Validation error = 34.23%

Analyze the Results

  • Training error 0.000.000.00 means the model classifies all training samples correctly.
  • Validation error 34.2334.23%34.23 means the model performs poorly on unseen data.

This large gap indicates poor generalization.

What is Happening?

The model is likely overfitting the training data. It has memorized the training samples instead of learning general patterns.

Possible Mistakes Made by Mr. Gibson

  1. Overfitting the training data
    • Trees may have been grown too deep without pruning.
  2. Incorrect Random Forest parameters
    • Very deep trees.
    • Very small leaf size.
    • Large number of features considered at each split.
  3. Data leakage
    • Training and validation sets may not have been separated correctly.
    • Some information from the validation set may have leaked into training or vice versa.
  4. Poor validation data
    • Validation data may come from a different distribution than the training data.
  5. Class imbalance
    • One class may dominate the training set, leading to poor validation performance.
  6. Using only training accuracy
    • Focusing on training error instead of validation performance can be misleading.

How to Improve the Model

  • Limit tree depth.
  • Increase minimum samples per leaf.
  • Tune hyperparameters using cross-validation.
  • Use Out-of-Bag (OOB) error to estimate performance.
  • Ensure proper train/validation split.
  • Improve data quality and feature selection.

Question 09: K-Means Clustering​

(a) Steps of K-Means Clustering Algorithm

The K-Means algorithm partitions a dataset into K clusters such that each data point belongs to the cluster with the nearest centroid.

  1. Choose the Number of Clusters (K): Decide the number of clusters (K).
  2. Initialize Centroids: Randomly select (K) initial centroids (cluster centers).
  3. Assign Data Points
    • Calculate the distance (usually Euclidean distance) from each data point to every centroid.
    • Assign each point to the nearest centroid.
  4. Update Centroids
    • For each cluster, compute the new centroid as the mean of all points in that cluster.
Centroid=Sum of points in clusterNumber of points\text{Centroid}=\frac{\text{Sum of points in cluster}}{\text{Number of points}}Centroid=Number of pointsSum of points in cluster​
  1. Repeat
    • Repeat Steps 3 and 4 until:
      • No point changes its cluster, or
      • The centroids do not change.
  2. Output: The final clusters and their centroids.

Question 04: Random Forest​

(a) General principle of an Ensemble Method. What are Bagging and Boosting?

semester: 2019-2020 - Q: 7(a)

(b) Accuracy is a good performance metric for imbalanced dataset - Justify your answer

No, accuracy is generally not a good performance metric for an imbalanced dataset.

In an imbalanced dataset, one class (majority class) has significantly more samples than the other (minority class). A model can achieve very high accuracy by simply predicting the majority class all the time, even though it completely fails to identify the minority class.

Example:

  • Dataset: 1,000 samples
    • 990 are Negative
    • 10 are Positive
  • A classifier predicts all samples as Negative.

Then:

  • Correct predictions = 990
  • Accuracy = 990/1000 = 99%

Although the accuracy is 99%, the model fails to detect any positive cases, making it ineffective for many real-world applications such as fraud detection or disease diagnosis.

Better metrics for imbalanced datasets:

  • Precision – Measures how many predicted positives are actually positive.
  • Recall (Sensitivity) – Measures how many actual positives are correctly identified.
  • F1-score – Balances precision and recall.
  • ROC-AUC or PR-AUC – Evaluate model performance across different thresholds.

Accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced datasets because it is dominated by the majority class. Metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC provide a more reliable evaluation of model performance.

Question 05: Confusion Matrix + ROC Curve​

(a) what do you understand by underfitting and overfitting

Underfitting occurs when a machine learning model is too simple to capture the underlying patterns in the data. As a result, it performs poorly on both the training data and unseen test data.

Characteristics:

  • High training error
  • High testing error
  • Poor predictive performance

Causes:

  • Model is too simple
  • Insufficient training
  • Too few features

Example: Using a linear model to fit highly nonlinear data.

Overfitting occurs when a model learns not only the underlying patterns but also the noise and random fluctuations in the training data. It performs very well on the training data but poorly on new, unseen data.

Characteristics:

  • Very low training error
  • High testing/validation error
  • Poor generalization

Causes:

  • Model is too complex
  • Too many features
  • Insufficient training data
  • Training for too many iterations

Example: A very deep decision tree that memorizes the training dataset.

Difference Between Underfitting and Overfitting

UnderfittingOverfitting
Model is too simpleModel is too complex
High training errorVery low training error
High testing errorHigh testing error
Fails to learn patternsLearns noise along with patterns
Poor performance on both training and test dataGood performance on training data but poor on test data

Summary:

  • Underfitting: The model does not learn enough from the data.
  • Overfitting: The model learns too much, including noise, and fails to generalize to new data.

β1=∑(X−Xˉ)(Y−Yˉ)∑(X−Xˉ)2\beta_1= \frac{\sum (X-\bar X)(Y-\bar Y)} {\sum (X-\bar X)^2}β1​=∑(X−Xˉ)2∑(X−Xˉ)(Y−Yˉ)​β0=Yˉ−β1Xˉ\beta_0=\bar Y-\beta_1\bar Xβ0​=Yˉ−β1​Xˉ

The coefficient of determination is

R2=r2R^2=r^2R2=r2

where (rrr) is the correlation coefficient.

From the data,

r≈0.9713r\approx0.9713r≈0.9713

Therefore,

(c) iscuss a situation when you choose regression over classification

You should choose regression over classification when the target (output) variable is continuous (numeric) rather than belonging to predefined categories.

Situations where Regression is Preferred

SituationWhy Regression?Example
Predicting house pricesPrice is a continuous valuePredict a house price of $350,000
Forecasting temperatureTemperature can take any real valuePredict 28.5°C tomorrow
Estimating sales revenueRevenue is numericPredict monthly sales of $75,000
Predicting student's marksMarks are continuousPredict a score of 82.7
Estimating travel timeTime is measured numericallyPredict 45 minutes to reach a destination

Suppose a real estate company wants to estimate the selling price of a house based on:

  • Area
  • Number of bedrooms
  • Location
  • Age of the house

Since the output is a numeric value (e.g., ₹65,50,000), this is a regression problem.

If instead the goal is to predict whether the house will sell or not sell, the output has two categories ("Sell" or "Not Sell"), making it a classification problem.

Regression vs. Classification

RegressionClassification
Predicts continuous valuesPredicts categorical labels
Output is numericOutput is a class/category
Examples: price, salary, temperatureExamples: spam/not spam, pass/fail, disease/no disease
Algorithms: Linear Regression, Ridge RegressionAlgorithms: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, SVM, Naïve Bayes

Choose regression whenever the objective is to predict a continuous numerical value. If the objective is to assign data into discrete categories or classes, choose classification instead.

Question 09: K-Means Clustering​

(a) Describe k-fold Cross Validation

k-fold cross-validation is a model evaluation technique used to estimate how well a machine learning model generalizes to unseen data.

Steps

  1. Divide the dataset into k equal-sized subsets (folds).
  2. Select one fold as the test (validation) set.
  3. Use the remaining k−1 folds as the training set.
  4. Train the model and evaluate its performance on the test fold.
  5. Repeat the process k times, using a different fold as the test set each time.
  6. Compute the average performance (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall) over all k trials.

Advantages

  • Uses all data for both training and testing.
  • Reduces bias caused by a single train-test split.
  • Produces a more reliable estimate of model performance.
(b) Define Core Point, Boundary Point, and Noise Point

These terms are used in DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise).

  1. Core Point: A core point is a point that has at least MinPts neighboring points within a radius ε (epsilon).

    • Located in a dense region.
    • Used to expand clusters.

  2. Boundary (Border) Point: A boundary (border) point is a point that:

    • Has fewer than MinPts neighbors within ε.
    • Lies within the ε-neighborhood of a core point.

    It belongs to a cluster but cannot expand the cluster.

  3. Noise (Outlier) Point: A noise point is a point that:

    • Is neither a core point nor a boundary point.
    • Does not belong to any cluster.
    • Is considered an outlier.
